highlights.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
highlights.summary: The call comes amid growing concerns that AI models may become able to inflict serious damage worldwide.
body: The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored.
In an essay on Saturday, Dario Amodei said developing AI was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious" and companies and governments must be given time to address them.
Amodei proposed a three-point plan that includes independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation.

There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks, the most serious of which suggested there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

highlights.title: Perplexity trusts GPT-6 Astra with end-to-end systems
highlights.summary: Perplexity uses Astra to write communications, change software, and monitor production systems, and checks in much less frequently than with earlier models.
body: As an AI-powered answer engine, Perplexity is deeply focused on search and accuracy. Its ability to process large amounts of information is critically important. Johnny Ho, Cofounder and Chief Strategy Officer, observes that every time the model gets better at writing code, Perplexity’s search engine improves too. It becomes able to write better programs that search the web and internal information and summarize it very concisely.
But the real challenge, according to Johnny, is taking those informational aspects and applying them to real-world systems. Something made easier with GPT‑6 Astra.
For Johnny, one of the most useful applications of AI is testing code. With limited time to test manually, he asks GPT‑6 Astra to build a small testing program around an application.

The model generates realistic responses like those another service would send, for example, a language model API or a connector. By standing in for those services, the model can check how the application responds and test the workflow from start to finish.

highlights.title: Breville Eye Q toaster review: a ‘revolutionary device’ that makes perfect toast without me trying
highlights.summary: I toasted just about every kind of bread in Breville’s new Eye Q – and each slice came out perfectly toasted. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. It’s a centuries-old problem: how to prepare the perfect slice of toast.
body: The core technology of the toaster has changed little in the past 100 years. A coil of high-resistance wires is activated for a certain period, and the radiant heat from that coil warms and browns the bread. The only measure of doneness that a traditional toaster has is time, but, as anyone who has had burnt toast for breakfast knows, time is a very imprecise proxy.

Breville’s new Eye Q toaster aims to change that legacy. Rather than setting a clock to tick until toast pops out, the Eye Q actually “looks” inside the toaster at the bread to determine whether it is done, thanks to a heat-resistant optical sensor that flashes 10 times per second to monitor the browning process. Hence the gadget’s catch phrase: “We watch your toast so you don’t have to.”

“It took us 10 years to get this project right,” Tom Groundes-Peace, global category manager and head of research at Breville, said. Groundes-Peace likens the innovation to the electric car: while cars evolved over the last century, they were all variations powered by an internal combustion engine. Until the electric motor.

body: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.
This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.
Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.
They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

highlights.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
highlights.summary: President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report.
body: The Trump administration is sacrificing Americans’ health to build data centers, former EPA officials warn.

At the start of his term, Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, proclaimed his goal of making America “ the AI capital of the world ” through deregulation. Since then, Zeldin and the White House have rolled back dozens of rules on top of cutting staff and funding at the US EPA.

As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “ protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape.
“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA.”

highlights.title: Blizzard's MOBA Is Making An Unexpected Comeback
highlights.summary: At BlizzCon 2026, Blizzard Entertainment announced a new hero for Heroes of the Storm: Xal’atath. He’s coming to the game later this month, and could signal a larger return of support for the game.
body: World of Warcraft players will recognize Xal’atath as the Harbinger of the Void and a major player in the MMO’s recent Midnight expansion. Xal’atath will come to Heroes of the Storm's PTR next weekend, and is playable for those attending BlizzCon.

Xal’atath is the first new Heroes of the Storm character in nearly six years. The most recent release was Hogger in December 2020, a year after Blizzard ended active development on HotS. Blizzard indicated at BlizzCon that Xal’atath may not be a one-off; depending on player response, the company said it may consider adding additional heroes to the game.

Heroes of the Storm initially released in 2015 and was Blizzard’s answer to the multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) craze. The game featured heroes from across Blizzard's brands, with playable characters borrowed from Warcraft, StarCraft, Diablo, and Overwatch. While the genre had emerged in the custom game and modding communities of Warcraft 3, Blizzard’s official MOBA lagged behind games like League of Legends and Dota 2, never finding the same level of success as those titles.

highlights.title: Inside ‘Ah Girl,’ the Singapore Drama Built From a Director’s Own Childhood: ‘We Can’t Fly Without First Learning How to Walk’
highlights.summary: Ang Geck Geck Priscilla spent more than a decade making “Ah Girl” before she ever made “Ah Girl.” Three short films and a decade of festival labs later, the Singaporean director’s feature debut is a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival for its North American premiere, following wins…
body: Writing from a child’s vantage point meant deliberately withholding adult understanding rather than supplying it. Ang says she kept returning to a single question while drafting the script: what does Ah Girl see, feel and think is happening, rather than what the audience needs to be told. Children, she says, register far more than the adults around them assume. “She is absorbing everything,” Ang says of her protagonist. “I want the adults watching the film to try to understand the child.”

That dynamic sharpens around the film’s central dilemma, in which Ah Girl is asked to choose which parent she wants to live with. “Sometimes they are hoping to hear the answer that will make them feel better about themselves,” she says. “A seven-year-old should never have to carry that emotional responsibility.” She adds that the film returns throughout to the gap between listening to a child and making a child responsible for an adult’s decision: “The adults keep asking her what she wants, but very few of them actually stop to ask what she needs.”

highlights.title: ‘I love the boldness of modernism’: New York fashion week goes highbrow
highlights.summary: Georgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander Calder. Calvin Klein has taken a highbrow turn in the two years since Veronica Leoni took charge.
body: Leoni called this the “discipline of removal”. Her muse this season was Georgia O’Keeffe, an artist who the brand’s namesake founder admired. Klein bought O’Keeffe’s painting Summer Days in 1983 for $1m, subsequently donating it to the Whitney Museum. A checked pattern taken from O’Keeffe’s distinctive capsule wardrobe of utilitarian chic appeared on this catwalk as a wrap coat, hardware-free with a fabric belt and no buttons.

One nod to pop culture was allowed: a model in a crepe-back satin ivory slip dress, her blond hair scraped back by a simple headband, called to mind the late Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the iconic Calvin Klein employee who was launched back into the fashion conversation by Ryan Murphy’s Love Story earlier this year.

Over at the Michael Kors show staged in the sunny courtyard of the Museum of Modern Art, the first model was wearing glossy black disc earrings the size of potato crisps suspended from glinting stainless steel hooks. They looked like pieces from Alexander Calder’s huge mobile, Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, which hangs in the stairwell of the museum.

highlights.title: OpenAI just wants to win
highlights.summary: OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.
body: Two mathematicians at the heart of recent controversies tell The Verge how AI giants’ ‘childish’ rivalries are upending the field.

Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.
Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad?

This week, The Verge spoke with more than a dozen mathematicians, including Tristan Buckmaster and Andreas Thom, who are at the center of recent controversies surrounding OpenAI’s work in the field. Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.

This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem.

body: The McLaren driver hadn't appeared to be in contention for pole at any point of the session, but found a huge amount of pace on his final run to edge out championship leader Antonelli by 11 thousandths of a second.

Max Verstappen, who had surged into pole contention earlier in the session, edged out Lewis Hamilton for third after the Ferrari driver produced a strong recovery having crashed in final practice earlier on Saturday.

The remarkable nature of Norris' lap was further highlighted by a near-half second gap to his team-mate Oscar Piastri in seventh.

body: For the fashion set—and now, almost everyone, thanks to the popularity of Ryan Murphy’s Love Story —1990s-era Calvin Klein conjures images of Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, pencil skirts, and white orchids. Mid-2000s Calvin Klein, on the other hand, brings to mind one particular citrusy and exotic scent, housed in a sexy bottle, and with a sexy ad series to match. Who didn’t have or want Euphoria on their vanity, back then? Even a whiff of it smells like a night out before cell phones: indiscriminately androgynous and intoxicating—or as one Reddit user called it, “almost narcotic.”

As of now, Euphoria is so back —with a new, more intense and potent concentration and a slick campaign fronted by Rosalía (gone are the muscled male models and oiled chests of yore, it seems.) Moments after the Calvin Klein Collection runway show on Friday, the Grammy-winner and recent Vogue cover star said that Euphoria always reminds her of singing on stage or being behind the wheel of her car—two moments that make her feel euphoric.

Over the years, they've put out a number of excellent records, dabbling in…
body: Their new album Ow ∞, released this past Friday, represents perhaps the boldest reinvention of their sound, however. It’s unabashedly nostalgic-sounding, trading the glitchy modular drums and glossy dance production of Free Love for turn-of-the-century breakbeats and distorted guitars. At times, the songs recall bands like Soul Coughing and Blur, on tracks like “Hot Slob” and “Concrete Glen.” But don’t worry, there’s still plenty of bleeps and bloops and modern vocal production techniques to keep fans of past albums happy.
To celebrate the release of Ow ∞, Sylvan Esso agreed to answer our weekly questionnaire.

body: Editor’s note: After more than a decade, this is the last WIRED Security News This Week. “The roundup,” as we call it internally, started as a way to ensure that our readers knew about the latest key cybersecurity and privacy news even if we didn’t write about it ourselves. It was a simple way to highlight our own work and the wealth of other great journalism and research published in this realm every week.

Over the years, the roundup has developed a devoted following, and some editions have even become viral hits—which is honestly weird, but the cybersecurity community is great and weird, so it feels right. Rest assured that something new and exciting is coming in the roundup’s place, so stay tuned for that! For now, as always, stay safe out there.

Meta failed to catch roughly 350 AI child abuse ads, according to new research this week, including some that included images of real kids. In one case, a child depicted in an ad was a member of a European royal family. Lawmakers have said they intend to investigate, and the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office ordered the company this week to stop “allowing” AI child abuse ads.

highlights.title: Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI
highlights.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its "adherence to safety practices and commitments." In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to "pace the frontier" - jargon…
body: Dario Amodei proposed a three-step plan to ‘pace the frontier’ of AI development.

Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with government agencies to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” This step would focus on AI companies operating in democratic countries, but because passing laws and building regulatory infrastructure takes time, Amodei says that the industry should work together to create safety standards.

The third step would be the most challenging — getting authoritarian governments like those in China and Russia to agree to slow development and adopt a global set of AI safety standards. But he also says it’s crucial that the US and other democracies maintain a technological lead over China and other authoritarian regimes by limiting their access to high-powered chips and cracking down on things like distillation that allow companies to quickly catch up by training its AI to replicate the behavior of a more powerful model.

highlights.title: Anthropic CEO outlines plan to ‘pace the frontier’
highlights.summary: What would it actually look like to "pace the frontier"?
body: We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development. But what would that actually look like?

In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so. And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them.

The debate over AI safety and alignment intensified this week after researcher Jacob Coxon wrote that he’s resigning from Anthropic over concerns that the leading AI companies are “gambling with our lives” while the people building the technology “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” a claim repeated by others at Anthropic.

Amodei’s post doesn’t didn’t explicitly mention Coxon’s resignation or his concerns, but the CEO wrote that two things convinced him it’s time to take a more cautious approach to AI development: the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, and the fact that “AI has been advancing drastically faster” in recent months, particularly with its “growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”

highlights.title: ‘The balloons made me smile but his expression made me stop’: Harivansh Verma’s best phone picture
highlights.summary: While celebrating a religious festival on the banks of the Ganges, the Indian photographer captured the everyday struggle of a street vendor. It had been a sacred day for Harivansh Verma. It was the evening of Ganga Dussehra, the major Hindu celebration and gathering along the banks of the Ganges.
body: “Haridwar holds a lot of deeply spiritual memories for me and my family,” Verma says. “In Hinduism we believe taking a dip in the Ganges cleanses you of your sins. Devotees travel from across the country and the ritual baths go on continuously from sunrise until late into the night. The atmosphere is magnificent.”

It was early evening when Verma took a stroll along the shore, looking for moments to capture with his smartphone. “When I came across this young man, the balloons made me smile at first, but his expression is what made me stop.”

Verma didn’t know the man, and they exchanged few words, aside from asking permission to take the shot. “There was nothing out of the ordinary about him, but his expression clearly reflected the heavy weight of worry and responsibility he was carrying. The contrast between the exhausted look on his face and the cheerful smiley faces on the balloons felt like two completely different stories existing in one frame.”
Verma hopes people will have a similar experience looking at this image. “Maybe they’ll smile at first, but then spend a little longer looking at him and wondering about his story.”
